summary: Zinc carnosine (polaprezinc, zinc-L-carnosine) is a 1:1 chelate of zinc and L-carnosine used as a gastric mucoprotective agent for gastric ulcers and gastrointestinal mucosal disease. The usual dose is 75 mg twice daily. It adheres to ulcerated mucosa where it releases zinc (supporting tissue repair) and L-carnosine (an antioxidant), induces protective heme oxygenase-1, and exerts anti-inflammatory and free-radical-scavenging effects. It is widely used in Japan and as a supplement elsewhere but is not FDA-approved as a drug.
indications: Treatment and prevention of gastric ulcers
Gastritis and gastrointestinal mucosal injury (including after Helicobacter pylori infection or endoscopic procedures)
Supportive mucosal protection (e.g., adjunct in oral and GI mucositis in some settings)

dosage.n: Optimal regimen in clinical trials; total 150 mg/day

dosage.d: 75 mg twice daily alongside eradication therapy

admin: Take orally, with or without food; granules may be dispersed where available
Continue the recommended course to allow mucosal healing
Avoid concurrent gastric irritants such as NSAIDs and alcohol where possible
Space apart from products that strongly chelate zinc if absorption issues are a concern
moa: Zinc-L-carnosine is a chelate that adheres preferentially to ulcerated or damaged gastric mucosa and gradually releases its components locally. Zinc supports protein synthesis, cell proliferation, and tissue repair while stabilizing membranes, and L-carnosine provides antioxidant and free-radical-scavenging activity. Polaprezinc is a potent inducer of the anti-oxidative stress enzyme heme oxygenase-1, and it inhibits inflammatory and neutrophil-mediated mucosal injury, together promoting mucosal protection and ulcer healing.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to zinc, L-carnosine, or polaprezinc
relative: Significant renal impairment (risk of zinc accumulation)
Conditions where high zinc intake is undesirable (copper deficiency risk with prolonged high use)
monitor: Copper and zinc status with prolonged high-dose use

preg: There are limited human safety data. Use during pregnancy only if the potential benefit justifies the potential risk.
lact: There are limited data on excretion into breast milk; zinc is normally present in milk. Use with caution during breastfeeding.
renal: Zinc is partly renally handled; use with caution in renal impairment to avoid zinc accumulation, particularly with prolonged therapy.
hepatic: No specific hepatic dose adjustment is established; use with general caution in significant hepatic impairment.

moderate: Quinolone and tetracycline antibiotics - zinc can chelate and reduce their absorption; separate dosing
Penicillamine and other chelators - reduced zinc availability or altered metabolism
minor: Iron and calcium supplements - may compete with zinc absorption
Long-term high zinc - can reduce copper absorption (copper deficiency)
interactions.food: May be taken with or without food.
interactions.alcohol: Avoid - alcohol aggravates gastric mucosal injury.
interactions.diagnostics: Prolonged high-dose use may lower serum copper; monitor if used long term.

serious: Copper deficiency with prolonged high-dose use (anemia, neutropenia)

monitoring: Copper and zinc status with prolonged or high-dose use
Complete blood count if copper deficiency is suspected (anemia/neutropenia)
counsel: Take regularly as prescribed to help the stomach lining heal
Can be taken with or without food
Avoid alcohol and unnecessary anti-inflammatory painkillers
Separate from certain antibiotics (quinolones, tetracyclines) by a couple of hours
Report rash, persistent fatigue, or new infections with long-term use
pk: Mucosal protective effect over days of regular use
Local mucosal adhesion; limited systemic absorption of intact chelate

pearls: NOT FDA-approved as a drug (FDA regards it as a dietary supplement); authored from Japan product information and published reviews
Polaprezinc adheres to damaged mucosa and releases zinc (repair) plus L-carnosine (antioxidant) locally
Potent inducer of heme oxygenase-1, contributing to anti-oxidative mucosal protection
Useful adjunct for ulcer healing, including after H. pylori eradication or endoscopic dissection
Prolonged high-dose zinc can cause copper deficiency - monitor if used long term
missed: Take the missed dose as soon as remembered. If it is almost time for the next dose, skip the missed dose and resume the usual schedule. Do not double the dose.
overdose: Acute overdose data are limited. Excess zinc intake can cause nausea, vomiting, epigastric pain, and, with chronic excess, copper deficiency. Manage supportively; for large acute zinc ingestion provide symptomatic care and consider copper status. There is no specific routine antidote.
